events.title: Central African Republic: Overview of incidents affecting humanitarian workers (october 2026)
events.summary: Country: Central African Republic Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs Please refer to the attached file. Since January 2026, 96 incidents have affected humanitarian workers in the Central African Republic. In October, 12 incidents were reported, compared to 14 in September, a decrease of 14 percent. Out of 12 incidents recorded in October, six were criminal in nature, including three cases of theft, two robberies and one assault. For the first time in 2026, a humanitarian worker was killed in an incident involving armed individuals. Five other incidents involved restrictions including movement restrictions, requests for documentation, arrest, taxation, and a protest targeting an NGO. The Birao sub-prefecture was the most affected with four incidents, followed by Bangui with three incidents. The sub-prefectures of Bocaranga, Bossangoa, Alindao and Obo each recorded one incident. International NGOs were the most affected, with eight incidents recorded, followed by UN agencies and national NGOs with two incidents each. Since January 2026, the Vakaga prefecture remains the most affected, with 24 incidents recorded, followed by Bangui with 21 incidents and Haut-Mbomou with 17 incidents.

"That is how I got this leg injury," she says pointing to severe swelling on her left leg. Despite countless medical interventions, Leabune has endured a long and painful road to recovery. events.title: Somalia: FLER activation: IDP assessment and community consultations in Afgooye District, Lower Shabelle Region (21 September 2026)
events.summary: Country: Somalia Sources: Norwegian Refugee Council, SOS Children's Villages International Please refer to the attached file. Executive Summary Between 29 August and 13 September 2026, intensified security operations and armed confrontations in parts of Lower Shabelle, including Basra, Alifow, Baqdaad and Areer Mooge, displaced more than 860 households (approximately 5,100 people, including about 3,640 children) towards Afgooye and surrounding communities, according to cluster/ABC reporting. An estimated 620 children are currently out of school. SOS Children’s Villages Somalia conducted a field visit and community dialogue in four IDP locations in Lafoole (Waafi, Docol, Durdur and Takulo) to verify the presence of newly displaced families, understand education and protection needs, and identify potential FLER sites. The assessment identified 402 newly displaced households. Education is the most urgent gap: existing public schools are located approximately 1 km to more than 3 km from the settlements, and children who remain out of school face heightened risks of abuse, neglect, exploitation, child labour, family separation, early marriage and psychosocial distress. Immediate FLER activation is therefore strongly justified. FLER will provide safe, structured learning, psychosocial support, play and life-skills activities, foundational learning and protection identification and referral, while creating a pathway into neighbouring schools. Docol and Durdur IDP Community Centres are the priority FLER locations, covering multiple surrounding IDP subcamps.

events.title: World: Preparedness for the next crisis means planning for the one after it
events.summary: Country: World Source: ODI - Humanitarian Practice Network Giuseppe Saba As the escalation of hostilities in Lebanon in March 2026 intensified humanitarian needs and displacement, the ability to respond quickly depended in part on decisions made before the emergency. By 1 May 2026, UNHCR reported that, together with shelter sector partners, it had delivered relief items to more than 200,000 displaced people, largely using pre-positioned supplies. Additional support included 40 trucks carrying more than 317 metric tonnes of critical aid from Dubai . Preparedness enabled the response. Stocks, logistics infrastructure and multiple transport options were available before the operating environment deteriorated. This flexibility is increasingly essential in humanitarian logistics. Conflict can escalate while teams are responding to floods elsewhere; a disease outbreak can increase demand as border restrictions constrain supply; and disruption to a single transport route can affect operations far beyond the crisis that caused it. Overlapping emergencies place simultaneous pressure on the same people, supplies, funding and logistics networks. Preparedness must therefore preserve the capacity to adapt under pressure. That requires strategically positioned supplies, alternative routes and suppliers, visibility of available stocks, established cross-sector relationships, and mechanisms that link early warning to early action. These options need to be in place before a response is under strain. Prepare for crises that overlap Other operational lessons from the past six years began with Covid-19. events.title: Informing to protect: communities mobilized against mpox in the Republic of the Congo
events.summary: Country: Congo Source: World Health Organization Pointe-Noire, Republic of the Congo— Building trust is often the first step in delivering an effective public health message. In the port city of Pointe-Noire, Christelle Mgami, a community health worker in Ngoyo health district, has made this a priority in her mpox awareness activities. “To raise awareness among residents, we must first earn their trust. We need to know how to approach them, listen to their concerns and encourage them to report suspected cases," she says. Like Mgami, 24 community health workers have been mobilized to bring prevention messages closer to communities and strengthen disease surveillance. Their work includes informing families, answering residents’ questions and encouraging people to seek care promptly if they develop suspected symptoms. In the Republic of the Congo, mpox remains a public health concern. In 2026, 127 confirmed cases and one death were reported across six departments of the country. Pointe-Noire accounted for 113 cases, representing nearly 89% of all cases reported nationally. The disease is transmitted through close contact with an infected person or contaminated objects. It can cause fever and skin lesions. Recognizing the signs and symptoms, understanding the modes of transmission and knowing preventive measures can help people protect themselves and limit the spread of the disease. To support government efforts, the World Health Organization (WHO), with financial support from the Government of Japan, is working with health authorities to strengthen risk communication and community engagement. events.title: Three months on from Nepal's devastating floods, thousands of children face a new threat: winter
events.summary: Country: Nepal Source: UN Children's Fund KATHMANDU, 25 November 2026 – Nearly three months after the devastating floods that struck Nepal on 26 August, thousands of children and families remain on a long road to recovery. While floodwaters receded, a new crisis is emerging as winter approaches, threatening children who have already lost homes, belongings, schools and access to essential services. The floods along the Bhote Koshi River affected an estimated 84,270 people, including 32,021 children. The floods destroyed or damaged thousands of homes and washed away clothing, blankets and other essential household items, leaving thousands of children and families vulnerable to the harsh winter conditions ahead. In the hills and mountains of Nepal, winter temperatures can fall well below freezing, reaching -12°C in some areas. "Children are still living with the consequences of the floods every day," said Alice Akunga, UNICEF Representative to Nepal. "Many have lost homes, schools, belongings and a sense of normalcy. As winter sets in, the risks facing children will only increase. No child should have to endure freezing temperatures because a disaster took away everything their family owned. Urgent support is needed now to help children stay warm, healthy, protected and learning through the winter months." Three months after the floods, and following the initial humanitarian response, children's worries are far from over. For many children, the disaster did not end when the floodwaters receded. Egypt’s strategic geographic location at the crossroads of Africa and the Middle East has made it both a transit hub and a destination point for those escaping dire and difficult circumstances. Due to ongoing conflicts in neighboring countries and escalating regional instability, Egypt continues to receive unprecedented numbers of refugees and people on the move. The domestic economy had already been impacted by global economic challenges, growing tensions in the Red Sea, and intensified conflicts in neighboring countries, all factors that have further compounded the delicate economic context. Within this regional environment, instability in Sudan, Gaza, and Libya has contributed to sustained population movements into the country. Egypt’s approach to migrants, refugees, and asylum-seekers is grounded in full respect for human dignity and human rights, consistent with the country’s obligations under the 1951 UN Refugee Convention and the 1969 OAU Convention. Nairobi, 24 November 2026 – International non-governmental organisations working in Sudan remain alarmed by the escalating use of drones and its toll on civilians. According to the UN Human Rights Office, at least 2,230 civilians were killed between January and October 2026, more than 1,630 of them in drone strikes, and the toll is likely higher. Drone strikes also continue to damage the infrastructure civilians need to survive and to disrupt life-saving assistance. Recent incidents in Nyala and Khartoum have again put civilians, including humanitarian personnel, in harm’s way. On 19 November, multiple strikes reportedly hit the Al Mazad district of Nyala, South Darfur, a civilian area close to humanitarian premises. On 22 November, drone strikes in Khartoum damaged a UN premises in a residential neighbourhood while personnel were inside. These incidents are not isolated. This is the Forum’s seventh alert on drone strikes this year.
